q: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
p: A clustered index defines the physical row order (the table is the index); non-clustered indexes are separate structures pointing back to rows.
cmds: CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX ix ON orders(id); -- SQL Server
CLUSTER orders USING orders_pkey; -- PostgreSQL one-time
tip: InnoDB primary key is the clustered index.
a: A clustered index stores the table rows themselves in the order of the index key, so there can be only one per table. In MySQL InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index, and secondary indexes store the primary key value as their row pointer, which means a long primary key makes every secondary index larger and lookups need a second traversal. In SQL Server the clustered index is chosen explicitly. PostgreSQL has heap tables with all indexes non-clustered; the CLUSTER command reorders the table once but does not maintain it. Clustered ordering makes range scans on the key very fast because rows are adjacent, but random primary keys such as UUIDs cause page splits and fragmentation on inserts. I prefer compact, monotonically increasing keys for clustered storage, and I use secondary indexes, ideally covering ones, for other access paths.
f: Why do long primary keys hurt InnoDB?
Why are random UUID keys a problem?

q: What is index selectivity and cardinality, and why do they matter?
p: Selectivity is the fraction of rows a value matches; high-cardinality columns make better index candidates because they narrow results.
cmds: SELECT n_distinct FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename='orders';
tip: Low-selectivity indexes are often ignored.
a: Cardinality is the number of distinct values in a column, and selectivity is how few rows a typical value returns relative to the table. An index on a high-selectivity column, like an email or order ID, lets the database jump to a handful of rows. An index on a boolean or a status column with three values returns a large part of the table, so the planner often prefers a sequential scan because random index lookups would cost more. The optimiser relies on statistics, histograms and most common values to estimate this, so stale statistics lead to bad plans; I run ANALYZE after bulk changes. Low-cardinality columns can still be useful as the leading column of a composite index paired with a selective one, or in a partial index that covers only the rare value, such as unprocessed rows. I judge an index by its effect on real query plans, not by theory.
f: When is a low-cardinality index useful?
How do statistics affect the plan?

q: How do you find unused and duplicate indexes and safely remove them?
p: Check index usage statistics over a full business cycle, find overlapping definitions, then drop in a controlled change with a rollback plan.
cmds: SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan;
tip: Reset windows can hide seasonal use.
a: Every index slows writes, consumes storage and memory, and adds vacuum work, so unused ones are pure cost. In PostgreSQL I query pg_stat_user_indexes for indexes with zero or very few scans, and in MySQL the sys schema shows unused indexes. Statistics reset on restart or manual reset, so I observe over a complete business cycle, including month-end or seasonal jobs, before deciding. Duplicates and redundant indexes appear when one index is a prefix of another, for example an index on column A when another covers A and B. Unique and constraint-backing indexes must stay. Before dropping, I save the definition so it can be recreated, check replicas since usage may differ there, and drop with the concurrent option to avoid locks. In MySQL, I can make an index invisible first to test the effect without deleting it. Then I monitor query performance after the change.
f: Why watch a full business cycle?
What is an invisible index in MySQL?

q: What are the different index types in PostgreSQL: B-tree, hash, GIN, GiST and BRIN?
p: B-tree is the default for equality and ranges; GIN suits arrays, JSONB and full text; GiST handles geometric and nearest-neighbour; BRIN is tiny for naturally ordered huge tables; hash is equality only.
cmds: CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON events USING brin (created_at);
tip: BRIN needs physical correlation.
a: B-tree handles equality, range queries and ordering, and covers most needs. Hash indexes support equality only and are rarely preferred. GIN, the generalised inverted index, maps elements to rows and excels at containment queries on arrays, JSONB and full-text search, at the cost of slower writes. GiST supports overlap, geometry, range types and nearest-neighbour searches. SP-GiST helps with partitioned search spaces like prefixes. BRIN stores summaries of block ranges and is extremely small, ideal for huge append-only tables where values correlate with physical order, such as timestamps in a log table, but is useless if the data is randomly ordered. Choosing the right type depends on the operators in the query, so I verify with EXPLAIN that the index is used. Extensions add more, such as trigram indexes for fuzzy text matching.

q: What is an index-only scan and what prevents it in PostgreSQL?
p: The query is answered from the index alone without visiting the table, but only if the visibility map shows pages as all-visible.
cmds: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT total FROM orders WHERE customer_id=7;
tip: VACUUM keeps the visibility map fresh.
a: An index-only scan returns results straight from the index when it contains every column the query needs, avoiding heap lookups. In PostgreSQL there is a catch from MVCC: the index does not hold row visibility information, so the executor must consult the visibility map to know whether all rows on a heap page are visible to everyone. If pages are not marked all-visible, because of recent updates or because vacuum has not run, it must still visit the heap, and the plan shows many heap fetches. To enable index-only scans I design covering indexes using the INCLUDE clause for payload columns, and I make sure autovacuum keeps up on frequently updated tables. The benefits are less I/O and better cache use, particularly for large tables, while the costs are bigger indexes and slower writes. I check the Heap Fetches figure in EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm the benefit.
f: What does the visibility map record?

q: How do you use pagination efficiently: OFFSET versus keyset pagination?
p: OFFSET scans and discards rows so deep pages get slower; keyset (seek) pagination uses an indexed last-seen value and stays fast.
cmds: SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET 100000;
SELECT * FROM items WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;
tip: Order by a unique indexed key.
a: With OFFSET, the database must produce and discard all skipped rows, so page one hundred thousand is slow and the cost grows linearly with depth. Results can also shift between requests when rows are inserted. Keyset pagination, also called the seek method, remembers the last row's sort key from the previous page and asks for rows after it using a where clause, which an index can satisfy directly, so every page costs about the same. The sort must be on a unique, indexed combination of columns, so I include a tie-breaker such as the primary key in both the order by and the comparison, using row-value comparison where supported. The trade-offs are that you cannot jump to an arbitrary page number and the cursor must be passed to clients. For APIs and infinite scroll it is the better choice; OFFSET remains acceptable for small tables or shallow pages.
f: Why do you need a unique tie-breaker?
What do you lose with keyset pagination?

q: How do you speed up COUNT(*) on large tables?
p: Use estimates from statistics, maintain counters, count with index-only scans, or cache; exact counts require scanning visible rows.
cmds: SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE relname='orders';
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '1 day';
tip: Ask whether exactness is really needed.
a: In MVCC databases like PostgreSQL, a count must check row visibility, so it scans the table or an index; on a table with hundreds of millions of rows that is expensive. I begin by asking whether an exact number is needed. For approximate totals such as a UI showing about 1.2 million results, the planner statistics give a cheap estimate. If an exact figure is needed, options include maintaining a counter table updated by triggers or application logic, though that adds write contention; using materialised or summary tables refreshed periodically; counting over a narrow indexed range such as the last day; or using an index-only scan on a small index with a well-vacuumed table. InnoDB also scans, though it can pick the smallest secondary index. For analytics, a columnar store or a cached aggregate is often a better design than counting on the transactional database.
f: Why is count slow in PostgreSQL?

q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and IN versus EXISTS?
p: UNION removes duplicates by sorting or hashing; UNION ALL just appends. EXISTS can stop at the first match and is often better than IN for correlated checks.
cmds: SELECT id FROM a UNION ALL SELECT id FROM b;
SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM items i WHERE i.order_id=o.id);
tip: Default to UNION ALL if duplicates are impossible.
a: UNION combines results and removes duplicates, which requires a sort or hash over the whole result and costs time and memory; UNION ALL simply concatenates, so when I know the sets are disjoint or duplicates are acceptable I use ALL. For IN versus EXISTS, modern optimisers often rewrite both into semi-joins and produce the same plan, but the semantic differences matter. EXISTS short-circuits at the first match and handles NULLs predictably. NOT IN behaves unexpectedly when the subquery returns NULL, because the comparison becomes unknown and no rows are returned, so I prefer NOT EXISTS or an anti-join. For large lists of constants, IN with a values list or a join against a temporary table can be better. As always, I check the actual plan with EXPLAIN on realistic data instead of assuming one form is faster.
f: Why is NOT IN dangerous with NULLs?
When does UNION ALL matter for speed?

q: How do you optimise queries that use LIKE with wildcards or full-text search?
p: Leading wildcards cannot use B-tree indexes; use trigram indexes, full-text search indexes or a search engine.
cmds: CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm; CREATE INDEX ON users USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
SELECT * FROM docs WHERE tsv @@ to_tsquery('english','deploy & rollback');
tip: Prefix patterns can use B-tree with the right operator class.
a: A pattern like name LIKE 'abc%' can use a B-tree index because it is a range scan on a prefix, although in PostgreSQL with non-C collations I need the text_pattern_ops operator class. A pattern with a leading wildcard, like '%abc', cannot use a normal index because there is no ordered starting point, so the database scans the entire table. For infix matching and fuzzy search, PostgreSQL's pg_trgm extension with a GIN or GiST index breaks text into trigrams and accelerates LIKE, ILIKE and similarity queries. For natural-language search with ranking, stemming and stop words, I use built-in full-text search with a tsvector column and a GIN index, and keep it updated with a generated column or trigger. MySQL offers FULLTEXT indexes. When requirements include relevance tuning, typo tolerance and facets at scale, a dedicated search engine such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch is the right tool.

q: How do you handle bulk inserts and updates efficiently?
p: Batch rows, use COPY or multi-row inserts, disable unnecessary indexes temporarily, commit in chunks and avoid per-row round trips.
tip: Round trips dominate small inserts.
a: Row-by-row inserts from an application pay a network round trip, a parse and often a commit for each row. The fastest approach in PostgreSQL is COPY, which streams data in bulk; MySQL has LOAD DATA. Where those are not possible, multi-row inserts or prepared statements batched in a single transaction cut overhead dramatically. For very large loads, I load into an unlogged or staging table, then transform and merge into the target, and consider dropping or deferring secondary indexes and constraints until after the load, rebuilding afterwards, which is faster than maintaining them for each row. Commit in sensible chunks, perhaps tens of thousands of rows, to limit lock time, transaction log size and replication lag. For bulk updates, I batch by primary key ranges with short transactions to avoid long locks and bloat. After large loads I run ANALYZE so the planner has fresh statistics.
f: Why is COPY faster than inserts?

q: How do prepared statements and the plan cache affect performance and security?
p: Prepared statements parse once and bind parameters, saving planning time and preventing SQL injection; generic plans can misestimate skewed data.
cmds: PREPARE q(int) AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=$1; EXECUTE q(42);
tip: Always parameterise, never concatenate.
a: A prepared statement is parsed once and executed many times with bound parameters. This saves parse and sometimes planning time, and crucially separates code from data, which is the primary defence against SQL injection, so I always parameterise queries rather than concatenating strings. The performance subtlety is plan reuse. After several executions, PostgreSQL may switch to a generic plan that does not depend on the parameter value; when data is skewed, for example one customer has millions of rows and others few, the generic plan may be poor for some values. The setting plan_cache_mode lets me force custom plans per execution. With connection poolers in transaction mode, session-level prepared statements can break unless the pooler supports protocol-level prepared statements. In the application, ORMs and drivers often prepare automatically, so I check their configuration when diagnosing odd plan behaviour.
f: Why can transaction pooling break prepared statements?

q: What is MVCC in PostgreSQL and how does it cause bloat?
p: Each update creates a new row version; old versions remain until vacuum removes them, so heavy updates need vacuum capacity.
cmds: SELECT n_dead_tup, n_live_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='orders';
SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM orders LIMIT 1;
tip: Long transactions block cleanup.
a: Multi-version concurrency control lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other, because each transaction sees a snapshot. In PostgreSQL an update writes a new row version and marks the old one as dead for later transactions, and a delete only marks it. Dead versions stay in the table until vacuum can prove that no active transaction still needs them. If updates are frequent and vacuum cannot keep up, or a long-running transaction or a lagging replica with feedback holds back the cleanup horizon, the table and its indexes accumulate dead space, called bloat, which makes scans slower and wastes cache. Mitigation includes tuning autovacuum to be more aggressive for hot tables, avoiding long idle-in-transaction sessions, using fillfactor to enable heap-only tuple updates, and occasionally rebuilding with pg_repack or a concurrent reindex. Monitoring dead tuple ratios helps catch it early.

q: What is transaction ID wraparound and how do you prevent it?
p: Transaction IDs are 32-bit and wrap; vacuum freezes old rows to avoid data becoming invisible, and failing to vacuum can force the database into read-only shutdown.
cmds: SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;
tip: Alert well before 1.5 billion.
a: PostgreSQL uses 32-bit transaction identifiers, compared in a circular fashion, so each row's age relative to the current transaction must stay below about two billion. Vacuum freezes old rows, marking them as visible to all future transactions. If freezing does not happen, the system eventually stops accepting writes to protect data from appearing to vanish, which is a severe outage that requires single-user-mode vacuuming. Causes include autovacuum being disabled or too slow for large tables, long-running transactions or abandoned replication slots holding the horizon back, and prepared transactions left open. Prevention is to monitor the age of datfrozenxid and per-table relfrozenxid and alert at moderate thresholds, keep autovacuum healthy with sufficient workers and cost limits, kill stuck old transactions and drop unused replication slots. Large tables may need tuned freeze settings and scheduled manual vacuums in quiet hours.
f: What do abandoned replication slots cause?

q: How do you tune autovacuum for a hot table?
p: Lower scale factors per table, raise cost limit or workers, and monitor dead tuples and vacuum duration.
tip: Defaults suit small tables, not huge ones.
a: The default trigger is a fraction of the table, twenty percent dead rows, which for a table with a billion rows means hundreds of millions of dead tuples before vacuum starts. For large or hot tables I set per-table storage parameters: a much smaller scale factor and a fixed threshold, so vacuum triggers earlier and does smaller, steadier work. If vacuum is running but too slowly, I raise the cost limit or reduce the cost delay so it does more work per cycle, and increase the number of autovacuum workers and maintenance memory when many tables need attention. I watch pg_stat_user_tables for dead tuple counts, last autovacuum times, and pg_stat_progress_vacuum for running jobs, and check that long transactions are not preventing cleanup. For insert-only tables, the insert threshold setting matters for freezing and visibility map updates. Tuning is iterative, guided by metrics.
f: Why is the default scale factor bad for big tables?
How do you see vacuum progress?

q: What is table and index bloat repair with pg_repack, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY and VACUUM FULL?
p: VACUUM FULL rewrites the table with an exclusive lock; pg_repack and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuild online with minimal locking.
tip: Avoid VACUUM FULL on live systems.
a: Plain VACUUM marks space reusable but rarely returns it to the operating system, so bloated tables stay large. VACUUM FULL rewrites the entire table into a compact file but holds an exclusive lock for the duration, blocking reads and writes, which is unacceptable on live production tables. Alternatives work online: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuilds an index while allowing normal operations, taking extra disk space and time; pg_repack creates a new copy of the table with triggers capturing changes, then swaps it in briefly under lock. These need free disk space about the size of the table and can add load and replication lag, so I run them in quiet periods and watch. Before repair, I confirm that bloat is real, using estimation queries or pgstattuple, and fix the cause, such as stuck transactions or insufficient autovacuum, otherwise it returns.
f: Why avoid VACUUM FULL in production?

q: How do you use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to find I/O problems?
p: Buffers show shared hits versus reads; many reads mean cache misses and disk I/O. Compare estimated and actual rows to spot bad statistics.
tip: Actual versus estimated rows is the first check.
a: EXPLAIN with ANALYZE executes the query and shows actual timings and row counts, and the BUFFERS option adds how many pages were found in shared buffers, as hits, versus read from the operating system or disk. A plan node with a high read count shows where I/O is spent; with track_io_timing enabled I also see time waiting on I/O. I first compare estimated rows with actual rows at each node: a large mismatch means stale or insufficient statistics, correlated columns or a misestimate, which leads the planner into bad join orders or scan choices. I look for sequential scans on large tables where an index should work, nested loops with huge outer row counts, sorts or hashes spilling to disk, shown as temp blocks, and repeated loops. Because ANALYZE runs the statement, I wrap data-changing queries in a transaction that I roll back. Fixes include indexes, statistics targets, query rewrites and work memory changes.
f: What do shared hit and read mean?
Why wrap DML in a rollback?

q: How does InnoDB use the redo log, undo log and doublewrite buffer?
p: Redo ensures durability, undo supports rollback and MVCC, and doublewrite protects against torn pages.
tip: Flush setting trades durability for speed.
a: InnoDB writes changes to the redo log before the data pages are flushed, so after a crash it can replay committed changes; the setting innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit decides whether each commit forces the log to disk, with the default of one giving full durability, and zero or two trading some durability for speed. The undo log stores previous versions of rows, which lets transactions roll back and lets consistent reads see older snapshots, implementing MVCC; long transactions make undo grow and slow purge. The doublewrite buffer protects against partial page writes during a crash by writing pages first to a safe area before their final location. Understanding these explains common behaviours: commit latency is dominated by log fsync, large transactions inflate undo and redo, and a redo log that is too small causes aggressive flushing and stalls. Tuning involves log file size, flush method and I/O capacity.

q: How do gap locks and next-key locks cause deadlocks in InnoDB at REPEATABLE READ?
p: Range scans lock gaps between index records to prevent phantoms; concurrent inserts into the same gap can deadlock.
cmds: SELECT * FROM t WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE;
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G -- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
tip: READ COMMITTED reduces gap locking.
a: At the default REPEATABLE READ level, InnoDB uses next-key locks, a record lock plus a lock on the gap before it, when scanning an index range with locking reads or updates, to prevent phantom rows. Two transactions can each lock a gap and then both try to insert into it; because gap locks do not conflict with each other but do block inserts, they wait on each other and deadlock. These situations appear around unique-key checks, range updates and delete-then-insert patterns. I diagnose with the latest detected deadlock section of the engine status or the deadlock logging option, which shows the statements and locks. Mitigations include keeping transactions short, accessing rows in a consistent order, using more selective indexes so fewer gaps are locked, switching to READ COMMITTED where phantom protection is not required, and adding retry logic in the application, since deadlocks are normal and recoverable.
f: What does a gap lock protect against?
Why should apps retry on deadlock?

q: How do you choose between MySQL replication formats and what is GTID replication?
p: Row-based replication is the safest; GTIDs give each transaction a global ID, making failover and replica repointing much simpler.
tip: Use ROW format and GTIDs.
a: Statement-based replication logs SQL statements and is compact, but nondeterministic functions and some statements can produce different results on replicas. Row-based replication logs actual row changes, which is deterministic and safe, with larger logs for bulk updates. Mixed switches automatically. Today row format is the standard. GTIDs assign every transaction a globally unique identifier, so a replica tracks which transactions it has executed instead of binary log file names and positions. This makes failover and topology changes much easier: when promoting a replica or repointing others, auto-position figures out where to continue, avoiding manual position arithmetic and the errors it invites. GTIDs also help detect errant transactions that exist on a replica but not the source. I combine GTID with semi-synchronous or group replication for stronger durability and monitor replica lag and errors continuously.

q: How do you perform online schema changes in MySQL with gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change?
p: These tools create a shadow table, copy data in chunks while capturing changes, and swap tables atomically with minimal blocking.
tip: Always test with dry-run first.
a: Altering a large table can lock it or take hours. Online schema change tools avoid that. They create a copy of the table with the new structure, copy rows in small chunks to limit load, and keep the copy in sync with ongoing changes, pt-online-schema-change using triggers and gh-ost reading the binary log, which avoids trigger overhead and allows throttling and pausing. At the end they swap the tables with a quick atomic rename. I run a dry-run first, check disk space for the copy, set throttling based on replica lag and server load, and schedule the cutover at a quiet time. Considerations include foreign keys, which complicate things, tables without primary keys, and a plan to abort cleanly. Newer MySQL versions support many in-place and instant alters natively, so I check the algorithm available before reaching for a tool.
f: When is a native instant ALTER enough?

q: What are common causes of MySQL replication lag and how do you reduce them?
p: Single-threaded apply, large transactions, heavy replica reads, I/O limits and missing indexes on replicas; use parallel replication and smaller transactions.
tip: Large transactions serialise apply.
a: Lag appears when the replica cannot apply changes as fast as the source produces them. Common causes are single-threaded apply of a very write-heavy workload, which I address with parallel replication using multiple workers; large transactions such as bulk deletes or alters that take as long to apply as to run and block everything behind them, which I fix by batching work into smaller transactions; replicas with slower disks or less memory than the source; heavy analytical reads on the replica competing for resources; and tables lacking a primary key or suitable index, which forces full scans for each row event under row-based replication. I measure lag with replica status and heartbeat tables, since seconds-behind-source can be misleading. Applications that read from replicas must tolerate lag or use read-your-writes routing, and I alert on lag thresholds.
f: Why is a missing primary key harmful for replicas?
How do you handle read-after-write needs?

q: How do you size a database connection pool correctly?
p: Pool size should match what the database can run concurrently, often cores times two plus disks, not the number of clients; more connections increase contention.
cmds: SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;
tip: Smaller pools are often faster.
a: A database can only make progress on as many queries as it has CPU cores and I/O capacity; extra concurrent connections just add context switching, lock contention and memory use, so throughput drops when the pool is too large. A common starting formula is about twice the number of cores plus the number of effective disks, then I load test and adjust. The total across all application instances matters, so with many pods each configured with a pool of twenty, the database sees their sum. Therefore I size per-instance pools from a global budget, and use a server-side pooler such as PgBouncer or ProxySQL to multiplex many clients onto a few database connections. I set timeouts for acquiring connections, idle timeout, and maximum lifetime to recycle connections, and monitor wait time for connections in the application, which signals real saturation better than the pool size does.
f: Why can a bigger pool be slower?
How does the total across instances matter?

q: What are the PgBouncer pooling modes and their trade-offs?
p: Session mode holds a server connection per client; transaction mode releases after each transaction (best multiplexing, restricts session features); statement mode is rarely used.
tip: Transaction mode breaks session state.
a: PgBouncer sits between applications and PostgreSQL, accepting many client connections and mapping them to a small number of server connections. In session mode a client keeps a server connection until it disconnects, which is compatible with all features but gives limited multiplexing. In transaction mode the server connection is returned to the pool when the transaction ends, so thousands of mostly idle clients can share a few dozen server connections, which is the usual choice for web applications. The cost is that anything relying on session state does not work reliably: session-level advisory locks, temporary tables, SET commands that persist, LISTEN and NOTIFY, and in older versions protocol-level prepared statements. Statement mode releases after every statement and forbids multi-statement transactions. I monitor with SHOW POOLS and SHOW STATS, watch client wait times, and size default_pool_size to the database's capacity.

q: How do you find and handle idle-in-transaction sessions?
p: They hold locks and block vacuum; find them in pg_stat_activity and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
cmds: SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS age, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='idle in transaction' ORDER BY age DESC;
tip: A forgotten BEGIN can bloat the whole database.
a: A session that issued BEGIN and then stopped, perhaps because the application crashed, waited on an external call, or forgot to commit, stays idle in transaction. It keeps its locks, blocking other writers, and holds an old snapshot, which prevents vacuum from removing dead rows anywhere in the database, leading to bloat and eventually wraparound risk. I find these by querying pg_stat_activity for that state ordered by transaction age, and by alerting on the maximum age. The preventive control is idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, which terminates such sessions after a limit; I set a value appropriate to the application, maybe tens of seconds. In the application, I make transactions short, avoid making HTTP calls or waiting on users inside them, and make sure the framework releases connections in finally blocks. For immediate relief I terminate the oldest offender after confirming it is safe.

q: How do you handle connection storms after a database restart or failover?
p: Use jittered retries, connection limits, pooler queues and gradual ramp-up so clients do not overwhelm the recovering database.
tip: Thundering herd needs jitter.
a: When a database restarts or fails over, every application instance tries to reconnect at once, often with identical retry intervals, creating a thundering herd that can exhaust connection limits and CPU, slowing recovery or causing another failure. I mitigate it in layers. Clients retry with exponential backoff and random jitter, and their pools have bounded sizes and acquisition timeouts. A server-side pooler or proxy absorbs the reconnection burst by queuing clients while keeping the number of real server connections low. The database's maximum connections limit and reserved connections for administrators ensure I can still log in. Applications should fail fast and shed load or serve degraded responses instead of piling up requests. After failover, DNS or proxy endpoints should point to the new primary quickly, and caches and prepared statements should be re-established gradually. I rehearse failovers to see how the whole system behaves.

q: What is max_connections and what are the memory implications of raising it?
p: Each connection uses memory for backend state and work_mem per operation; raising limits without pooling risks out-of-memory and slowdowns.
tip: Pool instead of raising the limit.
a: In PostgreSQL each client connection is a separate backend process with its own memory for caches and state, and queries can allocate work_mem for each sort or hash node, so worst-case memory is connections times work_mem times operations per query. Raising max_connections to several thousand without thought can cause out-of-memory kills, heavy context switching and slower snapshot computation. Typical advice is to keep max_connections moderate, a few hundred, and introduce a pooler for scale. I also keep a few connections reserved for superusers. If applications really need many concurrent sessions, I check whether they hold connections idle, which a pooler can fix. MySQL uses threads with lighter per-connection overhead but similar principles apply with per-thread buffers. When capacity is an issue, adding read replicas or vertical scale is better than allowing more simultaneous connections.

q: What is a replication slot in PostgreSQL and what risks does it carry?
p: A slot makes the primary retain WAL until the consumer confirms it; an inactive slot makes WAL pile up and can fill the disk.
cmds: SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS lag FROM pg_replication_slots;
tip: Alert on retained WAL size.
a: A replication slot guarantees that the primary keeps all WAL segments a consumer, such as a standby or a logical decoding client like a CDC tool, has not yet received. That prevents the replica from falling irrecoverably behind. The danger is that if the consumer disconnects or stops, the slot stays and the primary keeps accumulating WAL indefinitely, which can fill the disk and take the primary down. It can also hold back the cleanup horizon for logical slots. I monitor each slot's active status and retained WAL size, alert when they grow, and drop slots that belong to decommissioned consumers. Newer versions allow max_slot_wal_keep_size to cap retention, trading safety for the consumer by invalidating the slot rather than endangering the primary. Slots should be named and documented so owners are known.
f: How can a slot fill the disk?

q: How do you do a zero-downtime failover with a replicated database and what can go wrong?
p: Detect failure reliably, fence the old primary, promote the most caught-up replica, redirect traffic and rebuild; risks are split brain and data loss with async replication.
tip: Fence the old primary.
a: Failover has to detect that the primary is really down, which is hard because network partitions can look like failures. A coordination service or a tool such as Patroni uses a distributed lock so only one node can be primary. Steps are: ensure the old primary is fenced so it cannot accept writes, promote the most up-to-date replica, repoint clients through a virtual IP, DNS, proxy or service endpoint, and reconfigure the other replicas to follow the new primary. Risks include split brain, where two nodes accept writes and data diverges; data loss with asynchronous replication, as committed transactions not yet shipped are lost, which synchronous replication or quorum commit reduces at a latency cost; and application behaviour, like cached connections or DNS TTLs delaying cutover. Afterwards the old primary must be rebuilt or rewound. I rehearse failovers regularly and measure recovery time.

q: How do you route reads to replicas safely given replication lag?
p: Send only lag-tolerant reads to replicas, use read-your-writes strategies for recent writers, and monitor lag with fallbacks to the primary.
tip: Not all reads are equal.
a: Replicas offload read traffic but reflect the primary with a delay, so correctness depends on which reads can tolerate staleness. Reports, search pages and dashboards usually can; a user who just changed a setting and then reloads the page usually cannot. Strategies include routing a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, tracking the log position of the last write and only reading from replicas that have caught up to it, or using sticky sessions. Monitoring replica lag in time and bytes lets the router stop sending traffic to replicas beyond a threshold and fall back to the primary. Proxies like ProxySQL or application-level routing implement this. Also consider that replicas can have query conflicts with replay, and that heavy analytical queries on a replica can cause lag, so I separate reporting replicas from those serving user traffic.

q: What is the difference between logical and physical backups and when would you use each?
p: Physical backups copy data files and WAL for fast full restore and PITR; logical backups dump SQL or rows, which are portable but slower.
tip: Test the restore, not just the backup.
a: A physical backup copies the database's files, as a base backup, together with the write-ahead log, enabling fast restore of the whole cluster and point-in-time recovery to a chosen moment. It is version- and architecture-specific. A logical backup exports schema and data as SQL or a custom format, like pg_dump or mysqldump; it is portable across versions and platforms, supports restoring individual tables, and is useful for migrations and upgrades, but is slower to restore on large databases and gives a single point in time. In production I use physical backups with continuous WAL or binary log archiving as the primary disaster recovery method, using tools like pgBackRest or managed snapshots, and add periodic logical dumps for portability and small-scope recovery. All backups need encryption, offsite copies and regularly tested restores that measure real recovery time.

q: What is change data capture and how do logical decoding or binlog readers support it?
p: CDC streams row-level changes from the database log to downstream systems with low overhead, avoiding polling and dual writes.
cmds: CREATE PUBLICATION app_pub FOR TABLE orders;
debezium connector reading WAL via a replication slot
tip: Handle schema changes and slot lag.
a: Change data capture reads the database's transaction log to emit every insert, update and delete as an ordered event stream. Instead of polling tables or having the application write to both the database and a message queue, which risks inconsistency, CDC derives events from the committed log. In PostgreSQL, logical decoding exposes changes through a replication slot, and tools like Debezium turn them into messages on Kafka; MySQL tools read the binary log. Use cases are keeping search indexes and caches in sync, feeding analytics warehouses, building event-driven integrations and migrations with minimal downtime. Operational concerns include the slot retaining WAL if the consumer stalls, schema evolution needing coordinated handling, ordering and exactly-once semantics at the consumer, initial snapshots of existing data, and handling of large transactions. Monitoring consumer lag and slot size is essential.
f: Why is CDC better than dual writes?

q: How do you choose data types that affect performance and storage?
p: Use the smallest suitable types, avoid text for numbers, use timestamps with time zone appropriately and consistent types for join keys.
cmds: ALTER TABLE events ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint;
CREATE TABLE t (id bigint, created_at timestamptz, amount numeric(12,2));
tip: Mismatched types prevent index use.
a: Data types affect storage size, memory use, index size and speed. Smaller types mean more rows per page and better cache efficiency, so I choose integer sizes to fit the realistic range but with growth in mind, because changing an integer primary key to bigint later on a huge table is painful. I store numbers as numeric types, not strings, dates as proper date or timestamp types, and use fixed-point decimals for money rather than floating point. Join and foreign key columns must have identical types, otherwise implicit casts can prevent index usage. Text columns of unbounded size should avoid being in frequently scanned wide tables; large values are stored out of line. Enumerations or small lookup tables can replace repeated long strings. UUIDs are convenient but larger and random, so ordered variants help index locality. Good type discipline early prevents expensive migrations.
f: Why must join columns have identical types?

q: What are the trade-offs of UUIDs versus auto-increment integers as primary keys?
p: Integers are compact and ordered; UUIDs are globally unique and safe to generate anywhere but larger and random unless time-ordered.
cmds: id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
tip: Consider UUIDv7 or ULID for ordering.
a: Auto-increment integers are small, fast to compare, ordered so inserts append to the right edge of the B-tree, and friendly to caches. Their downsides are exposure of record counts and guessable identifiers if exposed in URLs, and coordination difficulties when generating IDs across multiple writers or shards. UUIDs can be generated anywhere without coordination, are hard to guess and simplify merging data from different systems, but at sixteen bytes they enlarge every index referencing them, and random version-four values scatter inserts across the index, causing page splits, poor cache locality and write amplification. Time-ordered variants such as UUIDv7 or ULID combine uniqueness with roughly sequential inserts and mitigate most of that cost. In clustered storage like InnoDB the effect of random keys is especially strong. I choose integers for internal single-database tables and time-ordered UUIDs when distributed generation or opaque identifiers are required.
f: Why are random UUIDs slow to insert?

q: How do you design indexes and tables for multi-tenant applications?
p: Include tenant_id in keys and indexes, choose shared schema, schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant by isolation needs, and guard against noisy neighbours.
cmds: ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
tip: Lead with tenant_id in composite indexes.
a: There are three common models. A shared schema stores all tenants in the same tables with a tenant identifier column: it is the most efficient and simplest to operate, but needs strict query discipline, often enforced with row-level security, and noisy neighbours can affect each other. Schema-per-tenant gives stronger separation and per-tenant customisation but becomes hard to manage with thousands of tenants because of catalog size and migrations. Database-per-tenant gives maximum isolation and easy per-tenant backup or placement, at the highest cost. For shared schema performance, I make tenant_id the leading column of primary keys and relevant indexes so queries touch only one tenant's contiguous data, and consider partitioning or sharding by tenant for very large ones. Large tenants may be moved to dedicated infrastructure. Rate limits and resource quotas protect against noisy neighbours.

q: When should you use JSONB columns versus relational columns?
p: Use JSONB for sparse, evolving or document-like attributes; use relational columns for core, frequently filtered fields needing constraints and joins.
cmds: CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (payload);
SELECT payload->>'plan' FROM accounts WHERE payload @> '{"active": true}';
tip: Promote hot JSON fields to columns.
a: JSONB offers flexibility to store attributes that vary between rows or change often without schema migrations, and PostgreSQL can index it with GIN and query it with containment and path operators. But overusing it loses relational advantages: constraints, foreign keys, type checking, straightforward joins, efficient statistics for the planner, and compact storage. Updating a small field rewrites the whole JSON value. My rule is that core entities and fields used in joins, filtering, sorting or aggregation belong in proper columns, while optional metadata, third-party payloads and rarely queried attributes can live in JSONB. If a JSON field becomes hot, I promote it to a real column, possibly a generated column from the JSON with its own index. Validation can be enforced with check constraints or application schemas. The hybrid approach gives flexibility where it is valuable and rigor elsewhere.
f: What do you lose with JSONB?

q: How do foreign keys affect performance and should you always use them?
p: They guarantee integrity but add checks on writes and need indexes on the referencing column; use them by default and remove only with a clear reason.
cmds: ALTER TABLE order_items ADD CONSTRAINT fk FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE;
tip: Index the child column.
a: Foreign keys enforce that referenced rows exist, preventing orphans, which is far cheaper than discovering corrupt data later. The cost is that inserts and updates to the child table must verify the parent, and deletes or key updates on the parent must check or cascade to children. PostgreSQL does not automatically index the referencing column, so without an index those parent-side checks scan the child table and can cause locking and slow deletes; I create indexes on foreign key columns. On extremely high-throughput systems, some teams drop foreign keys for sharded or very large tables and enforce integrity in application code, accepting the risk; in distributed databases cross-shard constraints may not be available. My default is to keep them, because integrity bugs are expensive, and remove them only where measurements show a real problem and compensating controls exist.
f: When might you drop foreign keys?

q: How does DynamoDB partitioning work and how do you avoid hot partitions?
p: Items are spread by partition key hash; uneven access concentrates load on one partition. Use high-cardinality keys, write sharding and adaptive capacity.
tip: Design keys from access patterns first.
a: DynamoDB distributes items across partitions by hashing the partition key, and each partition has throughput limits. If many requests target the same key value, for example a popular product or a date used as the key for all current writes, that partition throttles even if the table has spare capacity overall. Avoiding hot partitions starts with choosing a high-cardinality partition key that spreads access evenly, like user or device identifiers. For unavoidable hot keys, I use write sharding, appending a random or calculated suffix to the key and reading with a scatter-gather, or aggregating in a buffer before writing. Adaptive capacity and on-demand mode help absorb uneven loads but are not a fix for extreme skew. Caching hot reads in DAX or a cache layer also helps. Data modelling in DynamoDB begins with the access patterns, then keys and secondary indexes are designed to serve them.

q: What are the eviction policies in Redis and how do you choose one?
p: When memory is full Redis evicts by policy such as allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl or noeviction; choose by whether the data is a cache or a store.
tip: Never use noeviction for a pure cache.
a: Once Redis reaches maxmemory, its eviction policy decides what happens. Noeviction rejects writes with errors, appropriate when Redis is a primary data store and losing keys is unacceptable. Allkeys-lru evicts the least recently used keys among all keys, a good default for a cache, and allkeys-lfu favours frequency of use. The volatile policies only consider keys with an expiry set, so if few keys have TTLs they may find nothing to evict and fail writes. Volatile-ttl evicts those expiring soonest. Random policies exist but are rarely best. I choose based on role: cache means allkeys-lru or lfu with TTLs on entries, while queues or session stores need careful capacity planning and noeviction with alerts. I monitor memory usage, evicted keys, hit ratio and fragmentation, and size maxmemory below the machine's RAM to leave headroom for forks and buffers.
f: What should you monitor in Redis?

q: How do you prevent cache stampedes and keep a cache consistent with the database?
p: Use request coalescing, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate and explicit invalidation on writes; accept eventual consistency where possible.
tip: Two hard problems: invalidation and naming.
a: A cache stampede occurs when a popular key expires and many requests simultaneously miss and hit the database to rebuild it. Defences include a single-flight lock so only one request recomputes while others wait or serve the stale value, adding random jitter to expiry times so keys do not all expire together, and refreshing early or serving stale data while revalidating in the background. For consistency, the common pattern is cache-aside: read from the cache, on a miss load from the database and populate; on writes update the database and then delete the cache entry, which is safer than updating it because of races. There is always a short window of inconsistency, so I define acceptable staleness, set TTLs as a safety net, and for strict needs use write-through or event-based invalidation from change data capture. I monitor hit ratio and database load.
f: Why delete instead of update on write?

q: How does MongoDB indexing and the aggregation pipeline affect performance?
p: Compound indexes follow the equality-sort-range rule; the pipeline should filter and project early so stages can use indexes.
tip: Equality, sort, range.
a: MongoDB queries without a supporting index perform collection scans, so I create indexes matching query patterns. For compound indexes the guideline is equality fields first, then sort fields, then range fields, so the index serves filtering and ordering together. Explain with execution statistics shows documents examined versus returned; a large ratio indicates inefficiency. Covered queries, where the projection is satisfied by the index alone, avoid fetching documents. In aggregation pipelines, stage order matters: put match and sort stages early so they can use indexes, project only required fields, and limit before expensive stages like lookup or group, because later stages cannot use indexes in most cases and large groups may spill to disk. I avoid unbounded array growth in documents, watch the working set against RAM, and use the profiler to find slow operations. Shard keys need high cardinality and even distribution.

q: What consistency models exist in distributed NoSQL stores and how do you tune them?
p: Eventual, read-your-writes, strong and tunable quorum consistency; choose per operation based on correctness needs and latency.
tip: R + W > N gives strong reads in quorum systems.
a: Distributed stores replicate data across nodes, and consistency describes what a read can see after a write. Eventual consistency guarantees replicas converge but a read may return stale data briefly; it offers the best availability and latency. Strong consistency ensures reads reflect the latest committed write, at the cost of higher latency and reduced availability during partitions. Many systems let me tune per operation. In quorum-based systems like Cassandra with N replicas, writing to W and reading from R replicas with R plus W greater than N guarantees overlap and so the read sees the latest write. DynamoDB offers eventually consistent reads by default and strongly consistent reads at higher cost, and transactions when needed. I choose strong consistency for things like balances and inventory, and eventual for feeds and counters, always designing around the CAP trade-offs and the business impact of stale reads.
f: What does R + W > N guarantee?

q: How do you use RDS or Cloud SQL read replicas, Multi-AZ and high availability correctly?
p: HA standby is for failover durability, not read scaling; read replicas scale reads asynchronously; know the failover time and test it.
tip: Standbys do not serve reads in classic Multi-AZ.
a: People often confuse high availability with read scaling. A Multi-AZ or regional HA configuration keeps a synchronously replicated standby in another zone and promotes it on failure; in the classic model the standby does not serve traffic, so it adds resilience but not capacity. Read replicas replicate asynchronously and serve read queries, which scales reads but can lag and are not a guaranteed failover target unless promoted deliberately. Many managed services now offer variants that combine both. I plan for failover time, typically one to two minutes, with DNS endpoint changes, so applications must retry and reconnect, and I test by forcing a failover. Maintenance windows, minor version upgrades and storage scaling also can cause brief interruptions. I monitor replica lag, CPU, free storage and connections, and put cross-region replicas or backups in place for disaster recovery.

q: How do you tune IOPS and storage on cloud managed databases?
p: Match provisioned or burst IOPS and throughput to the workload; watch queue depth, burst balance and storage autoscaling limits.
tip: Burst credits run out.
a: Database performance on cloud storage depends on IOPS, throughput and latency limits, which vary by volume type and size. General-purpose volumes often provide a baseline proportional to size plus burst credits; once credits are exhausted, performance falls to the baseline and latency spikes, a common cause of mysterious slowdowns after a busy period. I watch metrics such as read and write latency, disk queue depth, IOPS against the provisioned limit and burst balance. If the workload sustains high I/O, I move to provisioned IOPS storage or increase volume size to raise the baseline. Memory matters too: a larger buffer cache reduces physical reads. I also check for instance-level throughput caps, which can be the limit rather than the disk, and enable storage autoscaling with a maximum to avoid running out of space. Query and index optimisation usually reduces I/O more cheaply than buying it.
f: What happens when burst credits run out?
Why can the instance limit I/O?

q: What is Amazon Aurora and how does its architecture differ from standard PostgreSQL or MySQL?
p: Aurora separates compute from a shared, distributed storage layer replicated six ways across three zones; replicas read the same storage, giving fast failover and low replica lag.
tip: Storage is shared, not copied per replica.
a: In standard engines each replica has its own copy of the data and replays the log. Aurora instead separates the database engine from a purpose-built distributed storage service that keeps six copies of the data across three availability zones and handles log application itself. Writers send log records, not full pages, to storage, reducing I/O. Read replicas attach to the same shared storage volume, so they need not replay data themselves; replica lag is typically milliseconds, and failover to a replica takes tens of seconds because there is no data copying. Storage grows automatically, and backups and snapshots are continuous and low impact. Trade-offs include cost, some vendor lock-in, and behaviour differences from stock engines, for example in extensions or tuning parameters. I still need good schema and query design, and I use cluster endpoints for writes and reader endpoints for load-balanced reads.
f: Why is Aurora replica lag so low?
What are the trade-offs of Aurora?

q: How do you monitor a managed database effectively with cloud-native tools?
p: Combine instance metrics, enhanced monitoring, performance insights and logs; alert on saturation and replication, not just CPU.
tip: Use Performance Insights for top SQL.
a: Managed databases hide the operating system but expose rich telemetry. I track the basics: CPU, memory, free storage, connections, IOPS, throughput and latency, plus replication lag and replica health. Performance Insights or Query Insights show database load broken down by wait events and top SQL, which is the fastest way to see what is consuming time. Enhanced monitoring gives operating system metrics at fine granularity. Logs, including slow query logs and error logs, are exported to the cloud logging service for search and alerting. Alerts focus on conditions that affect users or will soon: storage nearly full, connection count near the limit, sustained high load, replica lag, failed backups, and failover events. I also review recommendations from the provider, schedule maintenance deliberately, and keep dashboards that combine database metrics with application latency so correlation is quick during incidents.

q: How do you plan a major version upgrade of a production database with minimal downtime?
p: Test on a clone, check extension and application compatibility, use logical replication or blue-green deployments for near-zero downtime, and keep a rollback path.
tip: Rehearse with production-like data.
a: I begin by reading release notes for breaking changes, and testing the application against the new version in a staging environment restored from a recent production backup, including extensions, drivers, query plans and performance. In-place upgrades with pg_upgrade in link mode are fast but need downtime for the process and a tested rollback, such as keeping the old data directory or a snapshot. For near-zero downtime I build a new cluster on the target version, keep it in sync by logical replication, or use the cloud provider's blue-green deployment feature, then switch traffic after verifying data and performance, and keep the old cluster for a while as a fallback, with reverse replication if feasible. After the upgrade I run ANALYZE because statistics may not carry over, check query regressions, and monitor closely. Communication, a maintenance window and a clear go or no-go checklist are part of the plan.

q: How do you investigate sudden latency spikes on a database that otherwise looks healthy?
p: Correlate with locks, checkpoints, autovacuum, cache misses, plan changes, noisy neighbours and I/O limits using wait events and time-series.
cmds: SELECT wait_event_type, wait_event, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
tip: Wait events show where time goes.
a: I start by establishing the pattern: are spikes periodic, tied to deploys, batch jobs, or specific queries? Then I look at what sessions are waiting for, using wait events in pg_stat_activity or the Performance Schema in MySQL, which immediately separates lock waits, I/O waits and CPU. Periodic spikes often come from checkpoints flushing many dirty pages, autovacuum or autoanalyze jobs, backups, cron jobs or cache eviction after a deploy. Sudden plan changes after statistics updates or data growth can turn a fast query into a slow one; I compare plans with the pg_stat_statements history. Lock contention from long transactions or schema changes causes queues. I also check infrastructure: burst credits, throttling by the cloud provider, noisy neighbours, and connection storms. With the cause identified, I fix it specifically, for example spreading checkpoints, adjusting vacuum, adding an index, or limiting batch concurrency.

q: How do you set up and use slow query logging and query analysis tools?
p: Log queries over a threshold, aggregate with tools like pg_stat_statements, pgBadger or pt-query-digest, and fix the top offenders by total time.
tip: Rank by total time, not single slowest.
a: I enable slow query logging with a sensible threshold such as a few hundred milliseconds, and include enough context like duration, rows and the statement, being careful about sensitive literals in logs. Individual log lines are useful but aggregation is better. PostgreSQL's pg_stat_statements normalises queries and tracks calls, total and mean time, rows and buffer usage; pgBadger analyses logs into reports; MySQL has the slow log with pt-query-digest or the Performance Schema. I rank queries by total time consumed, calls times mean time, because a moderately slow query called a million times hurts more than one very slow report. For each top query I examine the plan, index usage, row estimates and call patterns, such as N+1 queries from the application, and fix by indexing, rewriting, caching or batching. After changes, I compare before and after metrics and keep the monitoring so regressions are visible.

q: How do you capacity-plan a database: CPU, memory, storage and growth?
p: Track trends in data size, working set, QPS and latency, project growth, and size for peak plus headroom with a plan for scaling up or out.
cmds: SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) FROM pg_catalog.pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 10;
tip: The working set should fit in memory.
a: I collect time-series for database size, growth by table, queries per second, latency percentiles, CPU, memory, I/O and connections, and look at daily and weekly peaks as well as the growth trend. Memory sizing aims for the hot working set and indexes to fit in cache, since misses go to disk. Storage planning includes data, indexes, WAL or binary logs, temporary files, backups and bloat, plus headroom for maintenance operations like rebuilding indexes that need extra space. I project growth with business forecasts, such as expected user numbers or new features, add a safety margin, and decide in advance triggers for action: when CPU stays above sixty percent at peak, or storage reaches seventy percent. Scaling options are vertical increases, read replicas, caching, archiving old data, partitioning, or sharding, each with different effort. I load test before big events and review capacity quarterly.

q: How do you archive or purge old data from huge tables without hurting production?
p: Partition by time and drop partitions, or delete in small batches with indexes, throttling and monitoring; archive first to cheaper storage.
cmds: ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2024_01;
DELETE FROM logs WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM logs WHERE created_at < now()-interval '1 year' LIMIT 5000);
tip: Dropping a partition is instant; deleting is not.
a: Large deletes create huge transactions, lock contention, bloat, long replication lag and heavy log volume. The best design is time-based partitioning: old data lives in its own partition, which I detach and archive or drop instantly with negligible overhead. If the table is not partitioned, I delete in small batches of a few thousand rows ordered by an indexed key, committing each batch, pausing between them to let replicas keep up and vacuum clean, and monitoring lock waits and lag, with the ability to stop at any time. Before deleting, I archive to cheaper storage like object storage in a columnar format, so compliance and analytical needs are met. Afterwards, I check for bloat and reclaim space if needed. Retention rules should be defined with the business and automated, and verified by tests, so data growth is controlled continuously and not through emergency cleanups.
f: Why is dropping a partition better than deleting?
How do you throttle batch deletes?

q: How do you handle a runaway query or lock pile-up in production?
p: Identify the blocker with the lock graph, assess impact, cancel or terminate it, and then fix the root cause with timeouts and query changes.
cmds: SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid))>0;
tip: Cancel before terminate.
a: When many sessions are waiting, the real problem is usually one blocker at the head of the chain. I find it using pg_blocking_pids or the sys schema's lock waits in MySQL, and look at what the blocker is doing, who owns it and how long it has run. If it is a long idle transaction or an ad hoc query, I try a gentle cancel of the query first, and terminate the session only if needed, aware that rolling back a large transaction can itself take time and keep locks. If it is a schema change waiting for a lock and queuing everything behind it, cancelling it clears the queue. Afterwards I address causes: set statement timeout, lock timeout and idle-in-transaction timeout; run DDL with a short lock timeout and retries; make application transactions short; and review the offending query for indexing or batching. A runbook with these queries speeds up the response.

q: How do you run safe load tests against a database before a launch?
p: Use production-like data volume and distribution, replay realistic workloads, ramp gradually, measure percentiles and resources, and isolate from production.
tip: Test with realistic data skew.
a: A useful database load test needs three realism points. The data must be production-sized and similarly distributed, because planner choices and cache behaviour change with scale and skew; restoring a masked copy of production is ideal. The workload must reflect real query mix, concurrency and think time, ideally by replaying captured traffic or by modelling the main transactions with a tool like pgbench, sysbench or a custom harness. The environment should match production instance types, storage and configuration, and be isolated so nothing touches live data. I ramp load gradually to find the knee where latency rises, record throughput, latency percentiles, error rates, and resource usage like CPU, I/O, locks and replication lag, and repeat after tuning to confirm improvements. Also test failure scenarios such as failover and replica loss under load. Results feed capacity plans and go or no-go decisions.
f: Why does data skew matter in tests?
What is the knee in a load curve?
